summary:
Aurora-1 is a 3D space mission design game for Windows that players can explore solo or with a crew of two to four. Players build a rocket, choose an orbit and scientific instruments, and plan how long the mission will take to develop and operate. Each choice has consequences. Adding an instrument increases launch mass and leaves less power for other systems.

In one mission, players aim a sensor at an archived NASA Terra/MODIS image of Lake Balkhash in Kazakhstan. They then point an antenna toward a ground station during a simulated communications window to send their observations back to Earth. Following a mission from the hangar to its first downlink helps beginners understand how rocket design, scientific goals and teamwork shape the results a mission can deliver.
details:
We developed Aurora-1, a 3D space mission design game for Windows. Players choose a scientific objective, assemble a rocket, select instruments and an orbit, and plan the mission’s development time and operational lifetime. The design choices carry into flight. Adding a fuel tank increases both fuel capacity and launch mass. During ascent, players can reduce thrust to manage heating, but doing so changes how quickly the rocket gains speed.

The mission continues after reaching orbit. In one scenario, players keep a sensor aimed at Lake Balkhash in Kazakhstan during an exposure, using an archived NASA Terra/MODIS image from July 15, 2024. They then aim an antenna to transmit the observations while a receiving station is within range. The game calculates these contact windows from the simulated orbit and published ground-station coordinates. NASA’s Blue Marble imagery gives players a view of Earth from the spacecraft.

Players can fly solo or divide four jobs among two to four people: flight director, commander, flight engineer and mission specialist. In smaller crews, players can switch between their assigned consoles from the same seat. A specialist might have observations ready to send while the flight director is still waiting for a station to come into range. That shared decision is part of the game’s educational value. Players see how the success of a scientific observation depends on choices made by several people, sometimes before launch.

We built Aurora-1 with Unity 6 and C#, using TCP networking for multiplayer and OpenAI Codex to assist with programming and testing. It runs on a Windows PC with a keyboard and mouse. We chose lightweight 3D models, bundled the NASA imagery for offline use, and included Russian, English and Kazakh interfaces. Our aim is to give first-time players room to experiment, repeat a mission after changing one decision, and see how that change affects the science they bring home.

Aurora-1 is a 3D space mission design game for Windows. Players choose a scientific objective, build a rocket, select an orbit and instruments, and plan the development schedule and operating lifetime. Those decisions follow the spacecraft into flight. An extra tank carries more fuel but adds mass, and a more demanding instrument competes with the transmitter for power. Players can fly manually, adjusting thrust as the rocket heats up, or use assisted controls while learning.

One mission asks players to observe Lake Balkhash in Kazakhstan. They track a target during an exposure using an archived NASA Terra/MODIS image from July 15, 2024. Once the observation is stored, they aim an antenna during a simulated pass over a receiving station such as Svalbard. The game uses published station coordinates to calculate when contact is possible. If the link drops halfway through, the crew must plan another pass to send the remaining data.

Players can fly solo or share four jobs in a crew of two to four. The flight director monitors ground contact, the commander flies, the engineer manages spacecraft systems, and the mission specialist operates the sensor and antenna. In smaller crews, two assigned consoles can be operated from one seat. Our creative approach was to turn a few seconds of ground contact into a shared task that gives each player a reason to care about the others’ decisions.

We built Aurora-1 with Unity 6 and C#, used TCP networking for multiplayer, and used OpenAI Codex to assist with programming and testing. We designed for a Windows PC with a keyboard and mouse, kept the download under 40 MB, bundled NASA imagery for offline use, and provided Russian, English and Kazakh interfaces. Our intended impact is to help beginners explore engineering trade-offs firsthand: change one design choice, fly again, and compare how much science reaches Earth.
